notes:
I've grouped these notes by verse. I read Enduring Word (Guzik), Matthew Henry, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Ellicott, Wesley's Notes, the Pulpit Commentary, Precept Austin, Calvin (only in search snippets; the full page wouldn't load), Constable, GotQuestions, Bible Hub study notes and two catholic.com pages. A few gaps:

- **Gill:** I didn't get Gill's notes on Leviticus 24 itself. The only Gill material below is his note on Exodus 21:24, used for v. 20.
- **No disagreement between Protestant traditions:** Nothing I read showed Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed or Lutheran teachers really disagreeing on this chapter. The differences are in emphasis, and I've marked them where they appear.
- **Not found at all:** No Lutheran, Orthodox or Bible Odyssey material, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching.

---

**vv. 1–2 (oil for the lamps)**
- Henry says this law first appeared in Exodus 27:20–21. It is here repeated, probably because it now began to be put in execution, when other things were settled. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_024.cfm
- Jamieson says "beaten" olive oil means cold-drawn, which is always of great purity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Lev/Lev_024.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the olives were beaten rather than crushed in a press, because pressing mixed in bits of fruit that discoloured the oil. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html
- Guzik notes that the lamps in the tabernacle – standing on the solid gold lampstand (Exodus 25:31-40) – were the only source of light for the tabernacle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- Wesley (Methodist) points out that the Hebrew says "the lamp," while v. 4 says "lamps": The seven lamps made all one lamp. He links this to the Blessed Spirit pictured in Revelation 4:5 as seven lamps of fire before the throne. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/24.htm

**v. 3 (outside the veil, evening to morning)**
- Guzik, quoting Rooker: The 'testimony' was a technical term for the Ten Commandments placed in the Ark. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- Guzik also notes that translations render "tend" in different ways, but the basic idea is doing all that is necessary to assure that the lamps are burning at the proper time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- The Pulpit Commentary takes "continually" to mean every night, from evening to morning. Aaron or his sons dressed the lamps each morning and lit them each evening. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html
- Precept Austin's sources say the phrase "lasting ordinance" refers to the unmitigating observance of this law in Israel's history until its typological fulfillment in Christ was realized. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_24_commentary

**v. 4 (the pure gold lampstand)**
- Wesley says it is called the "pure" lampstand partly because it was made of pure gold, partly because it was to be always kept clean. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/24.htm
- **What the light stands for (a difference of emphasis):**
  - Guzik: The continual light of the tabernacle pointed to the coming Messiah. Jesus never stopped being the light of the world (John 8:12). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
  - Henry (Puritan, Presbyterian): ministers are to hold forth the word, not to set up new lights, but, by expounding and preaching the word, to make the light of it more clear and extensive. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_024.cfm
  - Pulpit Commentary: the light symbolized the enlightening power of the Holy Spirit, which should illumine God's Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html
  - A Precept Austin source (quoted there, not named) says no one outside the holy place could see the light. It was there for God to see and for the priest to use. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60816/

**vv. 5–6 (twelve loaves in two rows)**
- Calvin (Reformed) says there is no doubt the twelve loaves refer to the twelve tribes, as if He would admit to His table the food offered by each of them. He also says the "two tenths" make one fifth of an ephah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-24.html
- Guzik: "showbread" literally means "bread of the face." This was bread associated with the presence of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- **"Rows" or "piles"?**
  - Wesley: Not one above another, but one beside another, as the frankincense put upon each, Lev 24:7, shews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/24.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary disagrees. It says the table was too small for rows, so the loaves were probably stacked in two piles of six, each loaf using over six pounds of flour. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html

**v. 7 (frankincense as a memorial portion)**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the frankincense was burned on the golden altar when the loaves were changed. It was probably held in cups placed on or between the piles, as Josephus describes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html
- Henry sees the twelve loaves as picturing All God's spiritual Israel, made a sweet savour to God through Christ. He links "memorial" to prayers rising before God (Acts 10:4). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_024.cfm
- Guzik quotes F. B. Meyer: "The two rows of six cakes foreshadow the unity and order of the Church; the fine flour, its holy, equitable character; the pure frankincense, the fragrance of Christian love." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/

**v. 8 (every Sabbath, a lasting covenant)**
- Guzik says God didn't want a stale communion with His people, but a continually fresh relationship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- The Pulpit Commentary describes the Sabbath changeover as recorded in the Mishnah: four priests carried in the new loaves and incense while four others took the old ones away. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html
- Constable says the daily lamps and the constant bread represented the daily sanctification of the people to their God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-24.html
- One sermon in the Pulpit Commentary treats the bread as a model for weekly church giving, linking it to 1 Corinthians 16:2. This is a homiletic application, not prosperity teaching. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html

**v. 9 (eaten by the priests in a holy place)**
- Ellicott says only eight of the priests' portions had to be eaten inside the sanctuary, and the showbread was one of them. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/24-9.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary counts about seventy-five pounds of bread for the priests each week. It notes this was the bread given to David in 1 Samuel 21:4–6. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html
- GotQuestions says Jesus used the David episode to show the Law was for man's benefit, and calls the showbread a wonderful picture of Jesus, the Bread of Life. https://www.gotquestions.org/bread-of-the-presence.html
- **Lord's Supper and Eucharist (where traditions differ):**
  - The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican-era homiletics) says Christ is the Church's spiritual food. It names the Lord's Supper as one way of feeding on him, but says he also feeds his people through the preached Word. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html
  - Catholic: a catholic.com video presents the bread of the presence as foreshadowing the Eucharist and the Real Presence. https://www.catholic.com/video/biblical-reason-the-eucharist-is-not-just-a-symbol
  - Catholic: a catholic.com article cites Brant Pitre on how the New Testament links Last Supper bread to Leviticus 24:5–7. It argues the showbread had to be unleavened (citing Leviticus 2:11). https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/arguing-with-the-orthodox-about-bread
  - The Pulpit Commentary disagrees on leaven. It says Scripture does not settle whether the loaves were leavened, since the showbread was not burned on an altar. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html

**v. 10 (son of an Egyptian father, a fight in the camp)**
- Henry: the trouble started with a quarrel. The mixed multitude of Egyptians that came up with Israel (Ex. 12:38) were in many ways hurtful to them, and this was one, they were often the authors of strife. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_024.cfm
- Jamieson: the "mixed multitude" suggests marriages like this were not infrequent. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Lev/Lev_024.cfm
- Calvin suggests many young women married Egyptians during the oppression to protect their relatives. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-24.html
- **Jewish tradition (reported, not endorsed):** Ellicott reports that the father was the taskmaster Moses killed (Exodus 2:11). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-24.html Guzik reports a rabbinic story that the fight began when the son tried to pitch his tent with his mother's tribe of Dan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- Wesley says he "went out" from Egypt as one of the mixed multitude, probably while Israel was near Sinai. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/24.htm

**v. 11 (blasphemed the Name; Shelomith)**
- Guzik defines blasphemy as attacking someone, especially God, with words. He suggests the man considered the God of Israel to be the same as the petty Egyptian gods. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- Wesley says he cursed Not the Israelite only, but his God also, as appears from Lev 24:15,16. Henry leaves both options open. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/24.htm
- Ellicott suggests a better rendering, "cursed the Name and reviled." He says the mother is named to guard the Hebrew women against intermarriage with heathen. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-24.html
- Ellicott adds that in the Second Temple period the phrase was read as "pronounced the Name," Hence it was enacted that the simple pronunciation of the Tetragrammaton was criminal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/24-11.htm
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible note, quoted at Precept Austin):** the two verbs may be one idea expressed with two words ("hendiadys"). The note gives three readings:
  1. verbal attack on Yahweh himself (Gerstenberger);
  2. a curse against the other man using Yahweh's name (Snaith, Wenham);
  3. simply saying the Name aloud (a standard Jewish explanation).
  
  Either way it violated Exodus 20:7 and 22:28. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60816/
- Precept Austin notes this is only the second story told in Leviticus. (The first was about Nadab and Abihu.) https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_24_commentary

**v. 12 (held until the LORD's will was clear)**
- Guzik: This was not a mob working outside the process of law. The question was whether the law applied to a foreigner. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- Wesley gives a different reason for the delay. God had said he would not hold such people guiltless, but had not declared how he would have them punished by men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/24.htm
- Jamieson: as the offense was a new one, he was put in ward till the mind of the Lord was ascertained. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Lev/Lev_024.cfm

**vv. 13–14 (outside the camp, hands on his head, stoning)**
- Ellicott: "outside the camp" was where the unclean lived and where criminals were executed (Hebrews 13:12–13). Jewish legal writers say the witnesses and judges declared, "Let thy blood be upon thine own head; thou hast brought this upon thyself." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-24.html
- Guzik ties the laying on of hands to the witness rule in Deuteronomy 17:6–7. He says stoning let the community take part, showing the man had sinned against the community too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- The NLT Study Note (cited at Precept Austin) says the gesture showed the witnesses' own innocence by symbolically transferring the guilt. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60816/
- Bible Hub's study notes see Christ in this scene: the sinless Christ was taken outside the camp (Hebrews 13:12) so that blasphemers could be forgiven. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/leviticus/24.htm

**v. 15 (whoever curses his God bears his sin)**
- Ellicott: having been asked about one case, God now lays down a general law for the punishment of blasphemers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-24.html
- Wesley: "bear his sin" means the punishment of it; shall not go unpunished. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-third-book-of-moses-called-leviticus/

**v. 16 (death for blasphemy, native or foreigner)**
- Calvin (Reformed) concludes that God's name must not be exposed to blasphemy with impunity among the sons of the Church. He also rejects blaming blasphemy on a fit of temper. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-24.html
- Wesley says the whole congregation stoned him To shew their zeal for God, and to beget in them the greater dread and abhorrence of blasphemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/24.htm
- Henry: some might think it hard to punish a man for a word, but God would teach them not to make light of such words. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_024.cfm
- Precept Austin: the death sentence had nothing to do with the fact that the man was half Egyptian. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_24_commentary
- Guzik quotes Rooker: if God required a foreigner to die, he would certainly not tolerate this among his own people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- The Pulpit Commentary (Clarkson) says this law made a lasting impression, so that no nation has been more reverent in its tone and spirit than the Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html

**v. 17 (murder punished by death)**
- Ellicott: the laws on murder and injury are repeated to show that, like blasphemy, they apply alike to Gentile and Jew. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-24.html
- Wesley gives another reason. The law is repeated because quarrelling, which here led to blasphemy, might in others lead to murder. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/24.htm
- Jamieson: these penalties were to be carried out by judges, not by the hand of private parties. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Lev/Lev_024.cfm
- Precept Austin: a distinction is clearly drawn in this passage between capital punishment and murder. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_24_commentary

**v. 18 (killing an animal: restitution)**
- Guzik: restitution showed the value of animal life, but the person was not a murderer and only had to make it good with money or another animal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/

**vv. 19–20 (eye for eye)**
- Guzik: God meant this as a limit – so no man or judge would set judgment merely as they pleased. He says it did not mean literally gouging out an eye, because the Law had a system of financial restitution. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
- Coffman: The "Lex Talionis" was not a law of personal revenge, but of public justice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/24-20.html
- Constable suggests the reminder of this law appears here because the whole congregation was responsible for the stoning. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/24-20.html
- **Literal or money penalty? (Gill, Baptist, on Exodus 21:24):** Gill says it is an open question. Josephus took it literally, while the Jewish writers generally in the latter (money penalties), as in the Targum. Gill adds that the Sadducees took it literally. https://www.studylight.org/bible/dut/lut/exodus/21-24.html and https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/nvl/matthew/5-38.html
- GotQuestions: it was the penal code, never intended to justify a personal code of revenge or vigilantism. https://www.gotquestions.org/law-of-retribution.html
- On Jesus' "turn the other cheek" (Matthew 5), Precept Austin's source says Jesus separates the government's duty to punish from the personal duty to love enemies. It adds that this in no way prohibits self-defense or the forceful protection of the innocent from harm. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_24_commentary

**v. 21 (animal versus human life)**
- Guzik: the passage teaches that crimes must be punished in proportion appropriate to the crime. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/

**v. 22 (one law for foreigner and native)**
- Calvin: the law covers foreigners so Israel would not think only Abraham's race was privileged. God shows that the whole body of the human race are under His care. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/leviticus-24.html
- Henry: strangers both benefit from this law and are liable to its penalties. He says this is why these laws are placed here. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_024.cfm
- G. Campbell Morgan, quoted at Precept Austin, says the principle protects the stranger from the possible in-justice of the home-born. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_24_commentary

**v. 23 (the sentence carried out)**
- Henry and Wesley (Wesley follows Henry almost word for word): This blasphemer was the first that died by the law of Moses. Stephen the first that died for the gospel, died by the abuse of the law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/24.htm
- Jamieson: stoning became the set punishment for blasphemy, which explains why Stephen was stoned on a false charge of it (Acts 7:58–59). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Lev/Lev_024.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary (Clarkson): the careful, patient process meant all could see that the man died because he had committed a grievous sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-24.html
- Guzik's application: God's laws are commands His people are expected to obey, even when obedience is difficult. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-24/
